newsitem.title: GERMANY: DASA on the mend, but days may be numbered. [CORRECTED 18:16 GMT]
newsitem.headline: DASA on the mend, but days may be numbered. [CORRECTED 18:16 GMT]

text.p: After suffering horrific losses, Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) is on the mend, but the plane maker's days as a single corporate entity may be numbered, analysts say.

DASA's four billion mark net loss in 1995 caused its parent, auto giant Daimler-Benz AG, to write the biggest red numbers in German corporate history and dogging former Daimler chief executive Edzard Reuter into retirement (corrects to clarify that Reuter retired).
In a bid to refocus group activities, Reuter's successor Juergen Schrempp has just won a long internal battle to re-absorb the profitable Mercedes-Benz car operation.

And, with DASA last year ditching its stand-alone aircraft production by dumping Dutch plane maker Fokker, which later collapsed, and selling out Dornier Luftfahrt, Schrempp may next turn his sights on his group's aerospace operations.
"It won't happen yet, but could come in two or three years," one German analyst, who declined to be identified, told Reuters on Tuesday.
DASA holds its annual news conference this Thursday, and is likely to say turnover fell slightly in 1996, orders jumped and it shed workers.
But bottom line numbers will have to wait until Daimler-Benz publishes group results in mid-April.

Analysts declined to estimate 1996 results, but DASA said last spring it expected group sales to fall to 13.2 billion marks from 15 billion in 1995. It forecast operating losses at 780 million marks, down from a 1.9 billion mark shortfall.
Nine-month results showed a surge in incoming orders -- mainly on the back of new Airbus business -- to 13.6 billion marks from 7.2 billion in the same period of 1995.
The European Airbus group, is a four-country consortium including Germany, France, Spain and Britain.
Analysts said they expected DASA management to say it is on course to post a small profit at the operating level this year.
The turnaround from the 1995 mega-loss will be helped this year by a surging dollar, cost savings and strong Airbus orders -- where rising production will start to kick in.

But even with DASA's finances recovering, its raison d'etre is being undermined by the competitive pressures -- intensified by the recent Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger -- which are flinging European aerospace companies into each other's arms.

Under a restructuring agreement struck in January by the four-country European Airbus group DASA's interest in the consortium will be converted into a shareholding in a limited-liability company by 1999.
That, analysts say, could be held as a simple direct stake by Daimler-Benz rather than through today's holding structure.
Co-operation in military projects like the Eurofighter 2000 combat jet -- facing tight defence budgets throughout Europe -- will increase too.
With profit margins wafer-thin, mergers will result despite political resistance in some countries.

Chris Partridge, analyst at Avmark in London, told Reuters that Daimler-Benz may also re-evaluate whether to hold on to its interest in DASA -- but only once the current upturn in the global aerospace market looks like maturing.
"At the very late end of the upcycle both orders and the business will look better," Partridge said, adding that now would be a bad time to sell.
Fat loss carryovers at DASA, which could help cut the tax bill at Daimler-Benz, rule out tinkering with its status for now at least, analysts said.
Even chief executive Manfred Bischoff, in an interview with Reuters last month, did not rule out that DASA itself may one day cease to exist.
But, he added: "I am not asking myself that question at the moment."
Bischoff said there was still a lot of hard bargaining to do before Airbus -- a grouping with France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace and Spain's CASA -- becomes a limited-liability company.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49-228-26097150
